title: React Rendering, Memoization and Code Splitting: Revision Notes
summary: Quick revision notes on what triggers a React re-render, how reconciliation and the virtual DOM work, when React.memo and other memoization pay off, and how to split code with lazy and Suspense.

chapters.title: What Triggers a Re-render
points: A render is React calling your component function to compute JSX; it is not the same as a DOM update, and a render can finish with zero DOM changes
Triggers: the component's own state setter, a parent re-rendering, and a changed value in a context it consumes; props changing is NOT a trigger by itself
A parent render re-renders all its children by default, even when their props are identical, unless the child is wrapped in React.memo

Mistake: mutating state in place (arr.push, obj.x = 1) then calling setState with the same reference. React compares with Object.is and bails out, so the UI does not update; always pass a new array or object

Interview Point: Does a prop change cause a re-render? Why does a child re-render when its parent re-renders with the same props? Is a render the same as a DOM update? Why does setState(sameValue) skip the update?

chapters.title: Reconciliation and the Virtual DOM
points: The virtual DOM is a lightweight tree of JS objects (React elements) describing the UI. Reconciliation diffs the new tree against the previous one, and React commits only the minimal DOM changes
Diff heuristics: elements of different types tear down the old subtree and remount (state is lost); elements of the same type update in place and keep state
Keys identify list items across renders. A stable unique id preserves item state and DOM; an array index breaks state when items are reordered, inserted or removed

Mistake: defining a component inside another component's body. Every render creates a new function type, so React unmounts and remounts it, losing state and focus. Changing a key deliberately is a way to reset a component's state

Interview Point: Why is a diff O(n) and not O(n^3)? What happens to state when the element type changes at the same position? Why is Math.random() a bad key? Is the virtual DOM faster than the real DOM?

chapters.title: React.memo in Practice
points: React.memo(Component) skips re-rendering when the props are shallow-equal (Object.is per prop) to the previous props. It only guards against parent-driven renders
Memo is defeated by new references created each render: inline objects, arrays and functions in props. Stabilise them with useMemo and useCallback so the shallow comparison passes
Memoized components still re-render on their own state changes and on context changes they consume. A custom comparator, React.memo(C, areEqual), is rarely needed

Example: const Row = React.memo(function Row({item, onSelect}) {...}); the parent passes onSelect={useCallback(fn, [])} so the Row skips renders. Passing {children} JSX created in the parent also breaks memo because the element is new each time

Interview Point: How does React.memo compare props? Why does memo fail when you pass an inline callback? Does memo block re-renders caused by state or context? When does a custom comparator make sense?

chapters.title: Memoization Trade-offs
points: useMemo caches a computed value and useCallback caches a function identity, both keyed by the dependency array. They cost memory plus a dependency comparison on every render
Worth it when: the calculation is genuinely expensive, the value feeds a memoized child or an effect dependency, or a list has many items. Not worth it for cheap calculations or primitives
Cheaper alternatives come first: move state down to the component that needs it, or lift static JSX up and pass it as children so it is not re-created when state changes

Mistake: wrapping everything in memo/useCallback. Wrong or missing dependencies cause stale closures, and the cache is not a semantic guarantee, since React may discard it. Measure with the React DevTools Profiler before optimising

Interview Point: When is useMemo slower than not using it? What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback? How can you avoid re-renders without memoization? How do you find the slow component?

chapters.title: Code Splitting with lazy and Suspense
points: Code splitting breaks the bundle into chunks loaded on demand using dynamic import(). React.lazy(() => import('./Page')) wraps a component whose default export is loaded the first time it renders

A lazy component must render inside <Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>. While the chunk loads, React shows the fallback; Suspense boundaries can be nested to control which part of the UI shows a loader
Split at route level first, then at heavy components such as modals, charts and editors. Splitting tiny components adds network requests for no gain

Mistake: no Suspense boundary above a lazy component makes the whole root suspend with no fallback, so nothing new shows until the chunk loads. A failed chunk load also rejects, so wrap with an Error Boundary to show a retry. Call lazy() at module top level, never inside a component, or it remounts every render

Interview Point: What does React.lazy require from the imported module? What happens if there is no Suspense boundary? Where should you split code in an app? How do you handle a chunk that fails to load?

chapters.title: Re-render and Performance Cheat Sheet
points: Re-render triggers: own state change, parent render, consumed context change. New reference in state means update; same reference means bail-out
Reconciliation: same type updates, different type remounts, stable keys for lists, never define components inside components
Performance order: measure with the Profiler, then move state down, then React.memo with stable props, then useMemo/useCallback only where needed
Splitting recipe: const Page = lazy(() => import('./Page')); <Suspense fallback={<Spinner/>}><Page/></Suspense>, with an Error Boundary around it for chunk failures
Interview Point: Explain the render phase versus the commit phase. Name three ways to stop an unnecessary re-render. When would you not memoize? How would you split a large route bundle?
